faq.a: The patient cannot mount a cellular response, so the attenuated pathogen replicates unchecked, causing disease.
faq.q: Why are live vaccines dangerous in SCID?

faq.a: Yes, a very low absolute lymphocyte count, absent thymic shadow and low immunoglobulins strongly suggest SCID, prompting urgent referral.
faq.q: Can SCID be diagnosed without flow cytometry?

faq.a: HSCT cures most patients if performed early with a suitable donor; outcomes are poorer with delayed transplant or active infections.

exam: A 3‑month‑old presents with chronic diarrhea, oral thrush and no thymic shadow – what is your immediate management? — Isolate, start IVIG, give prophylactic TMP‑SMX, begin broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and arrange urgent HSCT referral.

How does SCID differ from HIV infection in an infant? — SCID shows absent thymic shadow, profoundly low T‑cell count, and no maternal HIV antibodies; HIV may have normal thymus early and positive maternal serology.

A child with suspected SCID has a positive rotavirus vaccine stool PCR – what does this indicate? — Live vaccine strain infection confirms cellular immunity failure; stop further live vaccines and treat with supportive care.
Why is PEG‑ADA therapy used only in ADA‑deficient SCID? — It replaces the missing enzyme, correcting the metabolic block; other SCID types lack this defect and will not benefit.

What laboratory result would mislead you into thinking the child has X‑linked agammaglobulinemia instead of SCID? — Normal T‑cell count with low IgG could suggest agammaglobulinemia; SCID always has T‑cell lymphopenia.
In a low‑resource hospital without flow cytometry, which single test most strongly supports SCID? — An absolute lymphocyte count <2,500/µL in an infant <6 months combined with absent thymic shadow.
What are the contraindicated vaccines for a child with SCID? — All live attenuated vaccines (e.g., BCG, rotavirus, oral polio, measles‑mumps‑rubella).
During HSCT preparation, why must you avoid high‑dose steroids in SCID patients? — Steroids further suppress residual immunity and increase infection risk without improving engraftment.
ai.title: Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: SCID is a group of inherited disorders causing profound T‑cell and B‑cell dysfunction, leading to life‑threatening infections early in life. Prompt recognition, supportive care and definitive curative therapy are essential, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Absence of thymic shadow on chest X‑ray
Failure to thrive despite adequate nutrition
sections.p: SCID comprises rare genetic defects that block development of functional T lymphocytes; B cells are present but cannot be activated, and NK cells may be absent. Infants appear well at birth but develop severe, recurrent infections within weeks to months.

b: Absent thymic shadow on chest radiograph
sections.p: The immune defect is cellular (T‑cell) and humoral (B‑cell) with possible NK‑cell loss. Lymphocyte counts are markedly low; immunoglobulins are low or absent; vaccine‑derived live viruses can cause disease.

Patients suffer opportunistic, bacterial, viral and fungal infections; chronic diarrhea; and persistent oral thrush. In tropical settings, common pathogens include CMV, PCP, disseminated BCG, rotavirus vaccine strain, and opportunistic fungi.

Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion plus immunologic testing. In low‑resource hospitals, basic lymphocyte counts and immunoglobulin levels guide early decisions; referral for flow cytometry is ideal.

t.b: Is lymphopenia present? – Very low absolute lymphocyte count (<2,500/µL) supports SCID
Are levels markedly low for age? – Confirms humoral failure

t.a: Flow cytometry for CD3, CD19, CD56
t.b: What is the lymphocyte subset pattern? – T‑B‑NK‑, T‑B+NK‑, etc., defines SCID type
Is the thymic shadow absent? – Supports T‑cell deficiency
Which mutation is present? – Guides definitive therapy (enzyme replacement, gene therapy)

b: Strict isolation, avoid live vaccines, prophylactic TMP‑SMX for PCP, fluconazole for fungal prophylaxis
IVIG to supply passive antibodies (avoid in patients with severe IgA deficiency)
Enzyme replacement (PEG‑ADA) for ADA‑deficient SCID if available
Hematopoietic stem‑cell transplantation (HSCT) – curative; prioritize matched sibling donor, otherwise haploidentical or unrelated donor
Gene therapy for IL2RG or ADA defects where programs exist
sections.p: Management is three‑fold: protect from infection, provide immune reconstitution, and address the underlying genetic defect. In low‑resource settings, infection control and supportive care are critical while arranging transfer for definitive therapy.

b: Key clue: infant <6 months with severe infections, thrush, no thymic shadow
Distinguish from HIV (maternal antibodies, different lymphocyte pattern) and DiGeorge (facial anomalies, hypocalcaemia)
First emergency action: isolate, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, give IVIG, and arrange urgent referral for HSCT
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to recognise SCID quickly, differentiate it from other immunodeficiencies, and outline immediate steps.

whenToSeekHelp: New onset seizures or altered consciousness
